title: Hubble view of Messier 106
caption: The spiral galaxy Messier 106, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope with amateur data
celestial: M 106, Messier 106, NGC 4258 · constellation Canes Venatici · about 20 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, the Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA), and R. Gendler (for the Hubble Heritage Team). Acknowledgment: J. GaBany

recognition.text: Ranked #35 on ESA/Hubble’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: This view of Messier 106, also known as NGC 4258, blends Hubble observations with data from two amateur astronomers, Robert Gendler and Jay GaBany. It was Gendler who merged the Hubble data with his own observations to create the color image. M106, a spiral galaxy, lies just over 20 million light-years away in the constellation Canes Venatici.

Pictures like this show that professional and amateur astronomy can work together. Observations gathered by dedicated amateurs on the ground were blended with data from a space telescope to produce a single color portrait of the galaxy.
In astronomical terms, M106 is relatively nearby. Even so, the light captured here set out roughly 20 million years ago, so the galaxy appears as it was then rather than as it is today.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (6.59 x 5.15 arcminutes) and distance (20 million light years), the frame spans roughly 38,000 × 30,000 light-years. Its light set out about 20 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's ACS, WFC3 and WFPC2 observed in visible and near-infrared light, including a hydrogen-alpha filter, and the result was combined with amateur ground-based data. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures and combined datasets collect far more light than the eye can.
